blocks.label: Nitrogen
blocks.text: Nitrogen belongs to Group 15 (VA). It constitutes approximately 78% of the atmosphere and is obtained industrially by fractional distillation of liquid air. In the laboratory it is generated by heating ammonium nitrite solution: NH₄NO₂(aq) →(Δ) N₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).

blocks.head: Why N₂ Is Unreactive — Two Reasons
blocks.body: Molecular nitrogen (N₂) is one of the most unreactive diatomic gases. Two reasons account for this kinetic inertness:
items: 1. STRONG TRIPLE BOND: The N≡N bond has bond enthalpy +944 kJ/mol — one of the highest bond enthalpies known. Enormous energy is required to break it; reactions involving N₂ are kinetically inert at ordinary temperatures.

2. NONPOLAR BOND: Both atoms are identical; electronegativity difference = 0. The shared electrons are perfectly symmetrically distributed — no partial charges are present to attract electrophilic or nucleophilic reagents.

blocks.caption: Lewis structure of N₂ showing triple bond (one σ + two π) and lone pairs on each nitrogen atom
blocks.alt: N≡N with lone pairs, triple bond annotation, and bond enthalpy value +944 kJ/mol

blocks.head: Industrial and Practical Uses of N₂
blocks.body: The inertness of N₂ is exploited in many applications:
items: Dilutes O₂ in air — prevents sparks from igniting a large-scale fire
Blanket gas for hydrocarbon/edible oil shipments — protects from O₂ and moisture
Inert atmosphere for air-sensitive reactions in laboratory
Liquid N₂ (bp −195.8 °C) — used for cryogenic rapid cooling in food preservation and research

blocks.head: Haber-Bosch Process
blocks.body: Ammonia is manufactured industrially by combining nitrogen and hydrogen:
blocks.eq: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)    ΔH = −92 kJ/mol

blocks.head: Conditions and Reasoning
blocks.body: Conditions are carefully chosen to balance yield and rate:
items: Pressure ≈ 200 atm — high pressure favours product side (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas; Le Chatelier's principle)
Temperature ≈ 450 °C — compromise: lower temperature increases yield but decreases rate
Catalyst: iron (Fe) with K₂O/Al₂O₃ promoters — increases reaction rate without affecting equilibrium position

blocks.head: Displacement from Ammonium Salts
blocks.body: Heating ammonium chloride with calcium hydroxide (a strong base) releases ammonia:
blocks.eq: 2NH₄Cl(s) + Ca(OH)₂(aq) →(Δ) CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) + 2NH₃(g)

blocks.head: Bronsted-Lowry Interpretation
blocks.body: In the above reaction: NH₄⁺ acts as acid (donates H⁺) and OH⁻ acts as base (accepts H⁺). The strong base (OH⁻) drives NH₃ out of solution.

blocks.head: Collection and Identification
blocks.body: Laboratory collection of NH₃:
items: Dried over CaO (basic drying agent — does not react with NH₃)
Acidic agents like conc. H₂SO₄ or anhydrous CaCl₂ CANNOT be used — they react with NH₃
Collected by upward displacement of air (NH₃ is lighter than air)
Identification test: turns damp red litmus paper blue; has characteristic pungent smell

blocks.caption: Lab apparatus for NH₃ preparation: flask with NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ heated, CaO drying tube, inverted gas collection jar
blocks.alt: Round flask, delivery tube passing through CaO drying tube, into inverted collection jar

blocks.head: NH₃ as a Bronsted-Lowry Base
blocks.body: NH₃ acts as a base by accepting a proton (H⁺) from an acid using its lone pair on nitrogen:
blocks.eq:
NH₃(aq) + H⁺(aq) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq)
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)    Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵

blocks.head: Why NH₃ Is a Weak Base
blocks.body: NH₃ is a WEAK BASE because Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ is very small. The equilibrium lies far to the left — only a tiny fraction of NH₃ molecules are protonated at any time. This results in a low [OH⁻] and a mildly basic solution.

blocks.head: Geometry Comparison
blocks.body: Geometry changes when NH₃ accepts a proton:
items: NH₃: TRIGONAL PYRAMIDAL — one lone pair + three bonding pairs on N; lone pair compresses bond angle below 109.5° (actual ≈ 107°)
NH₄⁺: TETRAHEDRAL — the lone pair donates to H⁺ via a coordinate (dative) bond; no lone pairs remain; all four N-H bonds equivalent; bond angle exactly 109.5°

blocks.caption: Side-by-side comparison of NH₃ (trigonal pyramidal with lone pair shown) and NH₄⁺ (tetrahedral, all bonds equal, positive charge shown)
blocks.alt: NH₃ pyramid shape with lone pair on N, arrow to NH₄⁺ tetrahedral with four equal N-H bonds

items.q: Why is NH₃ described as a weak base rather than a strong base?
items.ans:
NH₃ is a weak base because its base dissociation constant Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ is very small. In the equilibrium:

NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

The equilibrium lies far to the left. Only a tiny fraction of NH₃ molecules accept a proton at any time → low [OH⁻] → mildly basic solution. A strong base would have essentially complete ionisation.

items.q: Explain why the geometry of NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral while NH₃ is pyramidal.
items.ans:
NH₃ has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on N → lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly → trigonal pyramidal shape (bond angle ≈ 107°).

NH₄⁺ forms when the lone pair of NH₃ donates to H⁺ (coordinate bond). No lone pairs remain → 4 equivalent bonding pairs → tetrahedral geometry (bond angle 109.5°).

items.q: Why cannot anhydrous CaCl₂ be used to dry ammonia gas?
items.ans: CaCl₂ reacts with NH₃ to form a stable complex CaCl₂·8NH₃. The ammonia gas is absorbed rather than dried. CaO (quicklime) is used instead — it is basic and does not react with NH₃.

blocks.head: Overview
blocks.body: Common oxides of nitrogen: N₂O, NO (and its dimer N₂O₂), NO₂ (and its dimer N₂O₄), and N₂O₅. Oxidation states range from +1 to +5. NO and NO₂ are collectively called NOₓ.

rows: Colourless gas; water-soluble; neutral; sweet smell; supports combustion; paramagnetic
Dental anaesthetic; propellant for whipped cream; synthesis of NaN₃
Colourless gas; slightly water-soluble; neutral; NO paramagnetic, N₂O₂ diamagnetic; oxidising AND reducing agent
Biochemical messenger (lowers blood pressure); synthesis of nitrosyl carbonyls
NO₂ = reddish-brown gas, paramagnetic; N₂O₄ = colourless; 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ (cool → N₂O₄, heat → NO₂); NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃ + HNO₂
Rocket propellant; Ostwald process for HNO₃; explosives

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Typo in oxide name (p.268)
blocks.wrong: The oxide NO/N₂O₂ is labelled 'Nitic oxide' in the Name column of Table 12.2.
blocks.reason: This is a typographical error. The correct IUPAC name for NO is nitrogen monoxide, commonly called nitric oxide.

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Table cross-reference (p.271)
blocks.wrong: Body text on p.271 refers to the nitrification/denitrification comparison table as 'Table 12.2'.
blocks.correct: The oxide properties table is Table 12.2; the nitrification/denitrification comparison table is Table 12.3.
blocks.reason: The in-text reference is one table number off — the nitrification/denitrification table is Table 12.3, not Table 12.2.

blocks.head: Natural Sources of NOₓ
blocks.body: Naturally occurring sources of nitrogen oxides:
items: Lightning — high energy dissociates N≡N bond: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g)
Volcanic eruptions
Forest and bush fires
Denitrifying bacteria in soil (produce N₂O)

blocks.head: Anthropogenic (Man-Made) Sources of NOₓ
blocks.body: Human activities that produce nitrogen oxides:
items: Combustion of fossil fuels in vehicle engines and power plants — N₂ + O₂ react at high engine temperatures (major source)
Chemical manufacturing plants
Biomass burning
Welding — high-temperature electric arc

blocks.label: Photochemical Smog
blocks.text: Photochemical smog (Los Angeles smog) is formed from NOₓ and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight (UV). It is OXIDISING in nature (unlike London smog which is reducing). Contains NO₂, ground-level ozone (O₃), and peroxyacyl nitrates (PANs).

blocks.head: Step-by-Step Reactions for Smog Formation
blocks.body: Formation of photochemical smog proceeds in five steps:
blocks.eq:
1. N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g)                [high engine temperature]
2. 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g)               [atmospheric oxidation]
3. NO₂(g) →(hν/UV) NO(g) + O(g)           [photodissociation]
4. O(g) + O₂(g) → O₃(g)                   [ground-level ozone formed]
5. RCH=CH₂ + O₃ → ... → RC(O)OONO₂       [PAN formed]

blocks.label: Peroxyacyl Nitrates (PANs)
blocks.text: PANs are a group of compounds with general formula RC(O)OONO₂. In peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN, the most common member), R = CH₃. PAN is a powerful lachrymatory (eye-irritating) agent and is toxic to plants.

blocks.head: Mechanism of PAN Formation
blocks.body: PAN formation follows a four-step free radical chain involving O₃, hydrocarbons, and NO₂:
items: Step 1: O₃ oxidises reactive hydrocarbon (RCH=CH₂) → aldehyde (RCHO)
Step 2: RCHO + OH• → acyl radical (RC•=O)
Step 3: RC•=O + O₂ → peroxyacyl radical [RC(=O)OO•]
Step 4: RC(=O)OO• + NO₂ → PAN [RC(=O)OONO₂]

blocks.caption: General PAN structure RC(=O)-O-O-NO₂ with R group label; PAN formation flowchart from O₃ + hydrocarbon through acyl radical to PAN
blocks.alt: PAN molecule structure and stepwise formation mechanism

blocks.head: Lahore Smog Composition
blocks.body: Lahore smog is a mixture of: VOCs, NOₓ, ground-level ozone (O₃), particulate matter (PM₂.₅), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂).

items.q: Write the five reactions involved in photochemical smog formation.
items.ans: 1. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO [engine combustion] 2. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ [atmospheric oxidation] 3. NO₂ →(hν) NO + O [UV photodissociation] 4. O + O₂ → O₃ [ground-level ozone] 5. RCH=CH₂ + O₃ → ... → RC(O)OONO₂ [PAN]

items.q: Why is PAN harmful to humans and plants?
items.ans:
To humans: PAN is a powerful lachrymatory agent — it irritates the eyes and mucous membranes. At high concentration it is also a respiratory irritant.

To plants: PAN causes chlorosis (yellowing) and leaf damage by inhibiting photosynthesis. Particularly harmful to crops such as spinach, tomato, and bean.

blocks.head: Structure of Catalytic Converter
blocks.body: A catalytic converter consists of:
items: Ceramic or metallic honeycomb-like monolith structure
Inner channels coated with washcoat of alumina (Al₂O₃) — provides very high surface area
Noble metals Pt (platinum), Pd (palladium), and Rh (rhodium) dispersed on the alumina layer
Metals can be recovered and recycled when the converter is replaced

blocks.caption: Cross-section of catalytic converter: honeycomb monolith channels, Al₂O₃ washcoat with Pt/Pd/Rh dots, arrow showing exhaust gas (HC/CO/NOₓ) entering and N₂/CO₂/H₂O exiting
blocks.alt: Honeycomb structure cross-section with metal catalyst dots on inner surface and gas flow arrows

blocks.head: Three-Way Catalytic Reactions
blocks.body: The converter handles three classes of pollutants simultaneously:
blocks.eq:
REDUCTION (NOₓ removal — Pt/Rh):
2NO(g) + 2CO(g) →(Pt/Rh) N₂(g) + 2CO₂(g)

OXIDATION (CO removal — Pt/Pd):
2CO(g) + O₂(g) →(Pt/Pd) 2CO₂(g)

OXIDATION (hydrocarbon removal — Pt/Pd):
2C₂H₄(g) + 6O₂(g) →(Pt/Pd) 4CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g)

blocks.head: Key Point
blocks.body: Conversion of NOₓ → N₂ is a REDUCTION (N: +2 → 0). Conversion of CO and hydrocarbons is OXIDATION. The converter is 'three-way' because it addresses three classes of pollutant simultaneously.

blocks.label: Nitrification
blocks.text: Conversion of ammonium (NH₄⁺) to nitrite (NO₂⁻) and then to nitrate (NO₃⁻) by nitrifying bacteria under aerobic conditions. These ions are absorbed by plants as essential nutrients.

blocks.label: Denitrification
blocks.text: Conversion of nitrate (NO₃⁻) back to atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) by denitrifying bacteria under anaerobic conditions. Important in wastewater treatment and in completing the nitrogen cycle.

blocks.head: Memory Aid
blocks.body: Denitrification is the 'demanding' process — both temperature and pH shift upward from nitrification values.

blocks.head: POSSIBLE BOOK ERROR — Nitrification pH upper limit (p.271)
blocks.wrong: Book states nitrification pH range as 6.5–8.0.
blocks.correct: Most standard references give optimum nitrification at pH 6.5–7.5; above pH 7.8–8.0 the nitrification rate drops significantly.
blocks.reason: An upper limit of 8.0 for nitrification is on the high side. Cross-check academy notes — if notes give 6.5–7.5 for nitrification, use that value in exams.

blocks.head: Nitrification Equations
blocks.body: Two-stage aerobic oxidation of ammonium nitrogen:
blocks.eq:
Stage 1 (Nitrosomonas):
2NH₄⁺(aq) + 3O₂(aq) → 2NO₂⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

Stage 2 (Nitrobacter):
2NO₂⁻(aq) + O₂(aq) → 2NO₃⁻(aq)

blocks.head: Denitrification Equation
blocks.body: Anaerobic reduction of nitrate back to nitrogen gas:
blocks.eq: 2NO₃⁻(aq) + 10e⁻ + 12H⁺(aq) → N₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)

items.q: Differentiate between nitrification and denitrification in terms of O₂ requirement, bacteria, and temperature.
Why is denitrification important in wastewater treatment?
items.ans: Wastewater contains high NO₃⁻ from domestic and agricultural runoff. Excess nitrate causes eutrophication in receiving water bodies. Denitrification converts NO₃⁻ → N₂ gas under anaerobic conditions, removing nitrogen from the wastewater before discharge — preventing algal blooms and oxygen depletion.

blocks.head: Basic Facts About Sulfur
blocks.body: Sulfur belongs to Group 16 (Chalcogens). Key physical data:
items: Electronic configuration: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴
Physical appearance: solid yellow crystalline non-metal
Melting point: 113 °C (honey-yellow liquid); boiling point: 445 °C
Common oxidation states: −2, 0, +2, +4, +6

blocks.head: Catenation and S₈ Allotrope
blocks.body: Sulfur prefers SINGLE BONDS over double bonds because 3p–3p π-bond overlap is poor (large atomic radius, diffuse orbitals). Instead, sulfur undergoes CATENATION — forming long S-S chains and ring structures.
items: Most stable allotrope: cyclo-octasulfur (S₈) — crown-shaped (puckered) ring of 8 sulfur atoms
Each S atom connected to its two neighbours by strong S-S single bonds
Stability of S₈ ring makes elemental sulfur unreactive toward water, dilute non-oxidising acids, and noble gases at room temperature

blocks.caption: 3D crown-shaped S₈ ring molecule showing all 8 sulfur atoms connected by single bonds in a puckered ring with alternating up/down positions
blocks.alt: Crown ring of 8 S atoms in chair-like puckered arrangement with S-S bonds labelled

blocks.head: Interesting Information
blocks.body: Other allotropes of sulfur: rhombic sulfur (most stable at room temperature, octahedral crystals), monoclinic sulfur (stable above 95.5 °C, needle-like crystals), and plastic (amorphous) sulfur formed by quenching hot liquid sulfur in cold water.

blocks.head: Why Sulfur Has Multiple Oxidation States
blocks.body: Sulfur is in Period 3 and has VACANT 3d ORBITALS. Electrons can be promoted from 3s and 3p into 3d orbitals, increasing unpaired electrons and allowing more bonds — expanding the octet beyond 8 electrons. Oxygen (Period 2) CANNOT do this.
items: Ground state [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ → 2 unpaired electrons → oxidation states −2 and +2
1st excited state [Ne] 3s² 3p³ 3d¹ → 4 unpaired electrons → oxidation state +4 (e.g. SO₂)
2nd excited state [Ne] 3s¹ 3p³ 3d² → 6 unpaired electrons → oxidation state +6 (e.g. SO₃, H₂SO₄)

blocks.caption: Orbital box diagrams for S: (a) ground state 3s² 3p⁴; (b) 1st excited state 3s² 3p³ 3d¹; (c) 2nd excited state 3s¹ 3p³ 3d². Oxygen ground state shown for contrast — no d orbitals available in n=2.
blocks.alt: Three rows of orbital box diagrams for sulfur showing electron promotion into 3d orbitals

sections.title: Stability of Oxidation States of Sulfur

items.title: Effect of pH
items.body: — Acidic conditions (low pH): reduced forms (H₂S, ox. state −2) are most stable. Basic/neutral conditions (high pH): oxidised forms (SO₄²⁻, ox. state +6) are most stable.

items.title: Thermodynamics vs. Kinetics
items.body: — SO₃ (+6) is thermodynamically the most stable sulfur oxide. But kinetic barriers prevent easy SO₃ formation at low temperature → SO₂ (+4) is commonly encountered under normal conditions.

items.title: Nature of the Compound
items.body: — Elements bonded to S affect stability. SO₄²⁻ is kinetically stable in acidic conditions due to strong O-S bonds.

items.title: Role of Catalyst
items.body: — Catalysts override kinetic barriers. V₂O₅ in the Contact Process dramatically increases the rate of SO₃ (+6) formation from SO₂ (+4) — achieving the thermodynamic product at a practical rate.

blocks.head: Most Stable Oxidation States at Extreme pH
blocks.body: Summary of pH effect on sulfur stability:
blocks.eq:
pH = 0 (strongly acidic) → H₂S (ox. state −2) most stable
pH = 14 (strongly basic) → SO₄²⁻ (ox. state +6) most stable

blocks.head: i. Combustion and Oxidation
blocks.body: Sulfur burns in oxygen with a blue flame:
blocks.eq:
S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) →(Pt, Δ) 2SO₃(g)
S(s) + 6HNO₃(l) → H₂SO₄(l) + 6NO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)   [oxidation by conc. HNO₃]

blocks.head: ii. Sulfur as Oxidising Agent — Reactions with Metals
blocks.body: Sulfur oxidises metals of lower electronegativity, forming sulfides (tarnishing):
blocks.eq:
2Ag(s) + S(s) → Ag₂S(s)   [silver tarnish]
Hg(l) + S(s) → HgS(s)
2Cu(s) + S(s) → Cu₂S(s)

blocks.head: iii. Cyanide to Thiocyanate
blocks.body: Sulfur converts cyanide (pseudohalide) to thiocyanate on heating:
blocks.eq: KCN(s) + S(l) →(Δ) KSCN(s)

blocks.head: iv. Reactions with Halogens
blocks.body: Sulfur reacts with different halogens to give different products:
blocks.eq:
S(l) + 3F₂(g) → SF₆(g)            [sulfur hexafluoride — very unreactive insulator]
2S(l) + Cl₂(g) → S₂Cl₂(l)          [disulfur dichloride — yellow liquid]
S₂Cl₂(l) + Cl₂(g) → 2SCl₂(l)      [sulfur dichloride — red liquid]

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — SCl₂ formation equation (p.274)
blocks.wrong: Book writes the third halogen reaction as: S(l) + SCl₂(g) → SCl₂(l) — chemically nonsensical (same compound on both sides; does not balance).
blocks.correct: S₂Cl₂(l) + Cl₂(g) → 2SCl₂(l). Disulfur dichloride (S₂Cl₂) reacts with excess Cl₂ to produce sulfur dichloride (SCl₂).
blocks.reason: The reactant should be S₂Cl₂ (product of the previous step), not 'S + SCl₂'. The book has a typographical/editing error in the reactant side.

items.q: Write the equations for the reactions of sulfur with Cl₂.
items.ans: 2S(l) + Cl₂(g) → S₂Cl₂(l) [yellow liquid] S₂Cl₂(l) + Cl₂(g) → 2SCl₂(l) [red liquid]

items.q: Why is sulfur unreactive at room temperature?
items.ans: Sulfur exists as stable cyclo-octasulfur (S₈) crown-shaped rings. The strong S-S single bonds within the ring require significant activation energy to break. Poor 3p-3p π-bond overlap means sulfur prefers the stable S₈ ring over reactive double bonds. At room temperature insufficient thermal energy is available to overcome this barrier.

sections.title: Uses of Sulfur and Its Compounds

blocks.head: Vulcanization
blocks.body: Sulfur forms DISULFIDE (S-S) cross-links between adjacent polymer chains of natural rubber. These cross-links:
items: Restrict chain slippage → increased rigidity and tensile strength
Prevent softening at high temperatures and brittleness at low temperatures
Improve durability — used in tires, hoses, gaskets, industrial rubber goods

blocks.caption: Two wavy polymer chains cross-linked by S-S bridges at multiple points showing restricted chain movement after vulcanization
blocks.alt: Two parallel polymer chains connected by multiple S-S cross-links

blocks.head: Sulfur in Fertilizers
blocks.body: Sulfur is an essential macronutrient for plant growth (component of amino acids cysteine and methionine). Applied as:
items: Ammonium sulfate — (NH₄)₂SO₄
Elemental sulfur — soil microbes convert it to soluble sulfate
Sulfur-coated urea
Gypsum — CaSO₄·2H₂O (provides Ca²⁺ and SO₄²⁻)

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Gypsum formula (p.275)
blocks.wrong: The book writes gypsum as CaSO₄·5H₂O.
blocks.correct: The correct formula for gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O (calcium sulfate dihydrate). CaSO₄·½H₂O = plaster of Paris; anhydrous CaSO₄ = anhydrite. No common calcium sulfate mineral has 5 molecules of crystallisation water.
blocks.reason: This is a factual error in the book. Gypsum always carries 2 water molecules per formula unit; the number 5 has no mineralogical basis.

blocks.head: Gunpowder Composition and Reaction
blocks.body: Composition by mass: 75% KNO₃ (oxidiser) + 15% charcoal/C (main fuel) + 10% sulfur (additional fuel — makes powder burn faster).
blocks.eq: 10KNO₃(s) + 3S(s) + 8C(s) → 2K₂CO₃(s) + 3K₂SO₄(s) + 6CO₂(g) + 5N₂(g)

sections.title: Role of Sulfur in Organic Synthesis

blocks.head: C-S Functional Groups
blocks.body: C-S bonds appear in biological, pharmaceutical, and industrial compounds. Key functional groups:
items: Thiols / mercaptans (–SH)
Thioethers (–S–)
Sulfoxides (–S=O)
Sulfones (–SO₂–)

blocks.head: Sulfur in Drugs
blocks.body: Sulfur-containing functional groups in important drug classes:
items: Sulfa drugs — antibacterial sulfonamides (first broad-spectrum antibiotics)
Penicillins and cephalosporins — beta-lactam antibiotics contain sulfur in their ring systems
Omeprazole (used in GERD — gastroesophageal reflux disease) — contains a SULFOXIDE (–S=O) group

blocks.head: Sulfur Dyes
blocks.body: Sulfur dyes are synthesized by thionation (sulfurization) of organic compounds containing nitro (–NO₂) or amino (–NH₂) groups. They contain sulfur linkages and give black, brown, khaki, blue, and green colours. Examples: sulfur black 1, sulfur blue, sulfur brilliant green.

blocks.head: Odorants and Fragrances
blocks.body: Mercaptans (thiols) are added to odourless natural gas at trace concentrations to make gas leaks detectable. Some thiols have pleasant odours at high dilution:
items: Thioterpineol — key component of grapefruit aroma
cis-Galbanum oxathiane — fragrant compound used in fine fragrances, soaps, shampoos, and shower gels
Many natural odorants are synthesized industrially as flavouring agents

blocks.head: Disulfide Bridges in Proteins
blocks.body: Disulfide bonds (S-S) form between cysteine residues in proteins, stabilising the 3D tertiary and quaternary structure (e.g. insulin, keratin). Breaking disulfide bonds unfolds the protein (denaturation).

blocks.head: Structure of H₂SO₄
blocks.body: Sulfuric acid has a tetrahedral geometry around sulfur:
items: Two S=O bonds (double bonds) — bond length 142.2 pm
Two S-O-H bonds (single bonds) — S-O bond length 157.4 pm; O-H bond length 97 pm
S=O bonds are shorter and stronger than S-OH bonds

blocks.caption: Lewis structure of H₂SO₄ showing tetrahedral geometry; S=O bonds (142.2 pm) and S-OH bonds (157.4 pm, O-H 97 pm) labelled; 3D ball-and-stick model alongside
blocks.alt: Tetrahedral H₂SO₄ with two S=O and two S-OH groups, bond lengths annotated

blocks.head: Physical Properties of H₂SO₄
blocks.body: Key physical data:
items: Molar mass: 98.08 g/mol
Colourless, viscous, odourless liquid
Melting point: 10 °C; Boiling point: 290 °C
Specific gravity (15 °C): 1.83 g/cm³
Hygroscopic — absorbs water vapour from air
Highly corrosive — causes severe chemical burns to skin, eyes, and clothing

blocks.head: i. Autoprotolysis (Self-Ionization)
blocks.body: H₂SO₄ undergoes self-ionisation and can act as a non-aqueous protic solvent:
blocks.eq: 2H₂SO₄(l) ⇌ H₃SO₄⁺(aq) + HSO₄⁻(aq)    K = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴

blocks.head: ii. Ionization in Water
blocks.body: H₂SO₄ is diprotic with very different pKa values for each step:
blocks.eq:
H₂SO₄(aq) → H₃O⁺(aq) + HSO₄⁻(aq)           pKa1 = −2   [strong — complete]
HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)  pKa2 = 1.92  [weak — partial]

blocks.head: iii. Dehydrating Agent (Conc. H₂SO₄)
blocks.body: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water from organic molecules:
blocks.eq:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → 12C(s) + 11H₂O(g)       [sucrose → carbon snake]
C₂H₅OH(l) →(conc.H₂SO₄, 170°C) C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l)    [ethanol dehydration]

blocks.head: iv. Reaction with NaCl
blocks.body: Concentrated H₂SO₄ displaces volatile HCl from its salt:
blocks.eq: NaCl(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄(s) + HCl(g)

blocks.head: v. With Active Metals — Dilute H₂SO₄ (Non-Oxidising)
blocks.body: Dilute H₂SO₄ — H⁺ is the oxidising agent (not SO₄²⁻) — gives H₂ gas with active metals:
blocks.eq: Zn(s) + dil.H₂SO₄(aq) → H₂(g) + Zn²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

blocks.head: vi. Oxidising Agent — Hot Concentrated H₂SO₄ Only
blocks.body: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidises metals and non-metals. S is reduced from +6 to +4 (produces SO₂):
blocks.eq:
Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(conc., hot) → ZnSO₄ + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O
Cu(s) + 2H₂SO₄(conc., hot) → CuSO₄ + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O

blocks.head: Important Distinction
blocks.body: Cu does NOT react with dilute H₂SO₄ — only hot concentrated acid oxidises it. Cold concentrated H₂SO₄ passivates Fe and Al (forms protective oxide layer). Dilute H₂SO₄ produces H₂ gas; hot conc. H₂SO₄ produces SO₂.

sections.title: Contact Process — Industrial Production of H₂SO₄

blocks.head: Importance
blocks.body: About 85% of all sulfur produced is used to manufacture H₂SO₄. H₂SO₄ is called the 'King of Chemicals' — its consumption level indicates a nation's industrial progress.

blocks.caption: Flowsheet of Contact Process: (1) Sulfur burner → SO₂; (2) Dust precipitator; (3) Washing/cooling tower; (4) Drying tower; (5) Arsenic purifier [Fe(OH)₃ shelves]; (6) Preheater; (7) Contact tower (V₂O₅ beds); (8) Heat exchangers; (9) Absorption tower → oleum; (10) Dilution → conc. H₂SO₄
blocks.alt: Full flowsheet of Contact Process with all stages labelled, gas flow arrows, and key conditions at each stage

blocks.head: Production of SO₂
blocks.body: Burning sulfur or iron pyrite to produce sulfur dioxide:
blocks.eq:
S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)                              ΔH = −297.03 kJ/mol
4FeS(s) + 6O₂(g) → 2Fe₂O₃(s) + 4SO₂(g)            [if iron pyrite used]

blocks.head: Removal of Catalyst Poisons
blocks.body: SO₂ from iron pyrite may contain As₂O₃ which poisons the V₂O₅ catalyst. Gelatinous Fe(OH)₃ in horizontal shelves absorbs As₂O₃:
blocks.eq: As₂O₃(g) + 2Fe(OH)₃(l) → 2FeAsO₃(l) + 3H₂O(l)

blocks.head: Oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃
blocks.body: Purified SO₂ and air, preheated to 420–450 °C, fed at 1–2 atm:
blocks.eq: SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g)    ΔH = −98.98 kJ/mol

blocks.head: V₂O₅ Catalyst Mechanism — Redox Cycle
blocks.body: V₂O₅ acts as a cyclic redox catalyst in two steps:
blocks.eq:
Step 1: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄   [V⁵⁺ reduced to V⁴⁺; SO₂ oxidised to SO₃]
Step 2: V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅           [V⁴⁺ reoxidised to V⁵⁺ by O₂ — catalyst regenerated]

blocks.head: Formation of Oleum and Final H₂SO₄
blocks.body: SO₃ cannot be dissolved directly in water — reaction is violently exothermic and produces acidic mist. Instead:
blocks.eq:
H₂SO₄(l) + SO₃(g) → H₂S₂O₇(l)     [oleum / fuming sulfuric acid]
H₂S₂O₇(l) + H₂O(l) → 2H₂SO₄(l)     [controlled dilution → desired concentration]

blocks.head: Industrial Uses of H₂SO₄
blocks.body: H₂SO₄ is used across virtually all chemical industries (H₂SO₄ acts as intermediate — rarely in final product):
items: Fertilizers — digest phosphate rock; manufacture (NH₄)₂SO₄; produce superphosphates
Metal extraction from ores (Cu, Ni, steel pickling)
Petroleum and coal refining; synthetic rubber; polymers; plastics
Pulp and paper; pesticides; herbicides; varnishes; dyes; pharmaceuticals
Explosives — nitration for TNT, nitroglycerin, nitrocellulose
Food industry — sugar, starch, corn syrup processing
Paint industry — manufacture of TiO₂ (white pigment)
Lead-acid storage batteries (35.67% H₂SO₄ solution)
Laboratory reagent

items.q: Why is SO₃ not dissolved directly in water in the Contact Process?
items.ans:
Dissolving SO₃ directly in water is violently exothermic and produces a dense acidic mist/vapour rather than a liquid solution — impossible to handle safely. Instead, SO₃ is absorbed in 98.5% H₂SO₄ to form oleum (H₂S₂O₇):

H₂SO₄ + SO₃ → H₂S₂O₇

Oleum is then carefully diluted with water to give H₂SO₄ of any desired concentration.

items.q: Explain how V₂O₅ acts as a catalyst in the Contact Process.
items.ans:
V₂O₅ acts as a cyclic redox catalyst:

Step 1: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄ [V⁵⁺ reduced to V⁴⁺] Step 2: V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅ [V⁴⁺ reoxidised to V⁵⁺]

V₂O₅ is continuously regenerated — it is a true catalyst. It lowers the activation energy for SO₃ formation, allowing the reaction to proceed practically at 420–450 °C.

items.q: Give three uses of sulfuric acid in industry.
items.ans:
• Fertilizer production — digests phosphate rock; manufactures (NH₄)₂SO₄
  • Petroleum refining — catalyst for alkylation and polymerisation
  • Lead-acid storage batteries — 35.67% H₂SO₄ solution

opts: It has a high specific heat
Its N≡N triple bond enthalpy is +944 kJ/mol
mcqs.exp: The N≡N triple bond has bond enthalpy +944 kJ/mol — one of the highest known. This makes N₂ kinetically inert at ordinary temperatures.

mcqs.q: The shape of the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) is:
mcqs.exp: NH₄⁺ has N bonded to 4 H atoms with no lone pairs → 4 bonding pairs → perfect tetrahedral geometry (bond angle 109.5°).

mcqs.q: In the Contact Process, the catalyst used to oxidise SO₂ to SO₃ is:
mcqs.exp: V₂O₅ (vanadium pentoxide) at 420–450 °C catalyses SO₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ SO₃ via a cyclic V⁵⁺/V⁴⁺ redox mechanism.
Nitrification (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) requires aerobic conditions, pH 6.5–8.0, and temperature 20–30 °C, carried out by nitrifying bacteria.

mcqs.q: The oxidation state of sulfur in H₂SO₄ is:
mcqs.exp: In H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +6. Sulfur is in its highest common oxidation state.

mcqs.q: The most stable sulfur species in an acidic environment (low pH) is:
mcqs.exp: Under acidic (low pH) conditions, reduced forms of sulfur (H₂S, oxidation state −2) are thermodynamically most stable.

mcqs.q: In a three-way catalytic converter, which metal pair catalyses the REDUCTION of NOₓ to N₂?
mcqs.exp: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂ uses Pt/Rh. Pt/Pd is used for oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate) formation is initiated when ozone reacts with:
mcqs.exp: PAN chain is initiated by O₃ oxidising the reactive hydrocarbon (alkene) → aldehyde → acyl radical → peroxyacyl radical + NO₂ → PAN.

mcqs.q: SO₃ is absorbed in 98.5% H₂SO₄ (instead of water) in the Contact Process because:
opts: SO₃ does not react with water
Dissolving in water is too slow
Direct dissolution produces a violent exotherm and acidic mist
mcqs.exp: Dissolving SO₃ directly in water is violently exothermic and produces an acidic mist/vapour — unsafe and impractical. SO₃ is absorbed in 98.5% H₂SO₄ → oleum (H₂S₂O₇), then diluted.

mcqs.q: Vulcanisation of rubber involves the formation of:
mcqs.exp: Sulfur forms S-S (disulfide) cross-links between adjacent polymer chains, restricting chain slippage and improving mechanical strength and durability.

mcqs.q: Sulfur can exhibit +4 and +6 oxidation states because:
opts: It has vacant 3d orbitals where electrons can be promoted
mcqs.exp: Period 3 sulfur has vacant 3d orbitals. Electrons from 3s/3p can be promoted into 3d (excited states) giving 4 or 6 unpaired electrons and allowing +4 and +6 oxidation states. Oxygen cannot do this.

mcqs.q: The formula for oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) is:
mcqs.exp: Oleum = H₂S₂O₇ (pyrosulfuric acid), formed when SO₃ dissolves in 98.5% H₂SO₄: H₂SO₄ + SO₃ → H₂S₂O₇.

mcqs.q: Composition of gunpowder by mass is:
mcqs.exp: Gunpowder: 75% KNO₃ (oxidiser) + 15% charcoal/C (main fuel) + 10% sulfur (additional fuel). Memory: 75-15-10.

saqs.q: List two reasons for the inertness of N₂.
saqs.a:
1. STRONG TRIPLE BOND: The N≡N bond has bond enthalpy +944 kJ/mol — one of the highest known. Enormous energy is required to break it; N₂ is kinetically inert at ordinary temperatures.

2. NONPOLAR BOND: Both N atoms are identical; electronegativity difference = 0. Shared electrons are perfectly symmetrically distributed — no partial charges to attract electrophilic or nucleophilic reagents.

saqs.q: Explain the laboratory preparation of ammonia with equation and collection method.
saqs.a:
Equation:

2NH₄Cl(s) + Ca(OH)₂(aq) →(Δ) CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) + 2NH₃(g)

Bronsted-Lowry interpretation: NH₄⁺ (acid) donates H⁺ to OH⁻ (base).

Drying: Passed through CaO. Acidic drying agents (CaCl₂, H₂SO₄) react with NH₃ and cannot be used.

Collection: Upward displacement of air (NH₃ is lighter than air).

Identification: Turns damp red litmus paper blue; pungent smell.

FeatureNitrificationDenitrification
DirectionNH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻NO₃⁻ → N₂
O₂AerobicAnaerobic
BacteriaNitrosomonas, NitrobacterDenitrifying bacteria
pH6.5 – 8.07.0 – 9.0
Temperature20–30 °C26–38 °C
RolePlant nutrition, soil fertilityWastewater treatment

saqs.q: Write the step-by-step reactions for photochemical smog and PAN formation.
saqs.a:
Smog reactions:

1. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO [engine combustion] 2. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ [atmospheric oxidation] 3. NO₂ →(hν) NO + O [UV photodissociation] 4. O + O₂ → O₃ [ground-level ozone] 5. RCH=CH₂ + O₃ → ... → RC(O)OONO₂ [PAN]

PAN mechanism:

  1. O₃ + RCH=CH₂ → RCHO (aldehyde)
  2. RCHO + OH• → RC•=O (acyl radical)
  3. RC•=O + O₂ → RC(=O)OO• (peroxyacyl radical)
  4. RC(=O)OO• + NO₂ → RC(O)OONO₂ (PAN)

saqs.q: Explain the construction and working of a catalytic converter.
saqs.a:
Construction:

  • Ceramic or metallic honeycomb monolith
  • Channels coated with Al₂O₃ washcoat (high surface area)
  • Pt, Pd, Rh dispersed on washcoat

Three-way reactions:

REDUCTION (Pt/Rh): 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂ OXIDATION (Pt/Pd): 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ OXIDATION (Pt/Pd): 2C₂H₄ + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 4H₂O

Harmful CO, NOₓ, and hydrocarbons are converted to harmless N₂, CO₂, H₂O.

saqs.q: Why is sulfur quite unreactive at room temperature?
saqs.a:
Sulfur exists as stable cyclo-octasulfur (S₈) — a crown-shaped puckered ring of 8 sulfur atoms connected by single S-S bonds.

  • Stable S₈ ring: Strong S-S bonds require significant activation energy to break — unavailable at room temperature.
  • Poor π-bond formation: 3p-3p orbital overlap in sulfur is poor (large atom, diffuse orbitals). Sulfur prefers stable single bonds and catenation over reactive double bonds.

Therefore, sulfur is unreactive toward water, dilute non-oxidising acids, and noble gases at room temperature.

saqs.q: How do the oxidation states of sulfur differ from oxygen? Give reason.
saqs.a:
Oxygen: limited to oxidation states −2, −1, 0 only.

Sulfur: can exhibit −2, 0, +2, +4, +6.

Reason: Sulfur is in Period 3 and has vacant 3d orbitals. Electrons from 3s and 3p can be promoted into 3d (excited states), giving 4 or 6 unpaired electrons → allows +4 and +6 oxidation states.

Oxygen is in Period 2 — no accessible d orbitals in n = 2 shell. Octet cannot be expanded → limited to lower oxidation states only.

saqs.q: Give two examples showing sulfuric acid as a dehydrating agent.
saqs.a:
1. Dehydration of sucrose (charring):

C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → 12C(s) + 11H₂O(g)

A black spongy mass of carbon (carbon snake) is produced.

2. Dehydration of ethanol:

C₂H₅OH(l) →(conc.H₂SO₄, 170°C) C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l)

saqs.q: Give two examples showing sulfuric acid as an oxidising agent.
saqs.a:
HOT CONCENTRATED H₂SO₄ acts as oxidising agent (S reduced from +6 to +4 → SO₂):

1. With zinc:

Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(conc., hot) → ZnSO₄ + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O

2. With copper (does NOT react with dilute H₂SO₄):

Cu(s) + 2H₂SO₄(conc., hot) → CuSO₄ + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O

saqs.q: What is the role of sulfur in vulcanization of rubber?
saqs.a:
Sulfur forms S-S (disulfide) cross-links between adjacent polymer chains of natural rubber. These cross-links:

  • Restrict chain slippage → increased rigidity and tensile strength
  • Prevent softening at high temperatures and brittleness at low temperatures
  • Improve durability — used in tires, hoses, gaskets, industrial rubber goods

saqs.q: Explain the V₂O₅ catalyst mechanism in the Contact Process.
saqs.a:
V₂O₅ acts as a cyclic redox catalyst in two steps:

Step 1 (Reduction of V₂O₅):

SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄

V⁵⁺ oxidises SO₂ to SO₃; itself reduced to V⁴⁺.

Step 2 (Regeneration of V₂O₅):

V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅

V⁴⁺ is reoxidised back to V⁵⁺ by atmospheric O₂ — catalyst regenerated.

Net result: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃, with V₂O₅ unchanged — a true catalyst.

saqs.q: Describe how photochemical smog differs from classical London smog.
saqs.a:
FeaturePhotochemical SmogLondon Smog
NatureOxidisingReducing
PrecursorsNOₓ + VOCs + sunlight (UV)SO₂ + smoke + fog
ComponentsNO₂, O₃, PANsSO₂, soot, H₂SO₄ droplets
Typical locationSunny, dry cities (e.g. Los Angeles, Lahore)Cold, humid industrial cities
Main sourceVehicle exhaustCoal burning

lqs.title: Q8(b) — Ammonia Preparation, Basicity, and Photochemical Smog
lqs.q: Describe the preparation and basicity of ammonia, and explain how NOₓ gives rise to photochemical smog and PAN formation.

parts.label: PREPARATION OF AMMONIA
points: Industrial — Haber-Bosch: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
Conditions: ~200 atm (high pressure favours product side — 4 mol → 2 mol gas), ~450 °C (compromise: rate vs. yield), Fe catalyst with K₂O/Al₂O₃ promoters
Lab — heating ammonium salt with strong base: 2NH₄Cl(s) + Ca(OH)₂(aq) →(Δ) CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃
Dried over CaO (not CaCl₂ or H₂SO₄); collected by upward displacement of air; tested with damp red litmus (turns blue)

parts.label: BASICITY OF NH₃
points: NH₃ acts as Bronsted-Lowry base by accepting H⁺ using its lone pair: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ — very small → equilibrium far to the left → only tiny fraction protonated → weak base
NH₃: TRIGONAL PYRAMIDAL — one lone pair + three bonding pairs on N; bond angle ≈ 107°
NH₄⁺: TETRAHEDRAL — lone pair donated to H⁺ via coordinate bond; no lone pairs remain; all four N-H bonds equivalent; bond angle 109.5°

parts.label: PHOTOCHEMICAL SMOG FORMATION
points: Source of NOₓ: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO at high engine temperature; then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ in atmosphere
Photodissociation: NO₂ →(hν/UV) NO + O
Ground-level ozone: O + O₂ → O₃ (harmful at ground level; different from protective stratospheric ozone)
Smog is OXIDISING — unlike London smog (reducing). Contains NO₂, O₃, and PANs

parts.label: PAN FORMATION MECHANISM
points: Step 1: O₃ + RCH=CH₂ → RCHO (aldehyde) — ozone initiates chain by oxidising alkene
Step 2: RCHO + OH• → RC•=O (acyl radical) — hydroxyl radical abstracts H from aldehyde
Step 3: RC•=O + O₂ → RC(=O)OO• (peroxyacyl radical) — acyl radical captures O₂
Step 4: RC(=O)OO• + NO₂ → RC(O)OONO₂ (PAN) — peroxyacyl radical combines with NO₂
In peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN): R = CH₃; general formula RC(O)OONO₂
PAN is a powerful lachrymatory agent (eye irritant) and toxic to plants

lqs.title: Q8(b) — Alternative: Contact Process and Chemical Properties of H₂SO₄
lqs.q: Give the flowsheet of the Contact Process for manufacture of H₂SO₄ and discuss the chemical properties of sulfuric acid.

parts.label: CONTACT PROCESS — FOUR STAGES
points: Stage 1 — Burning: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297.03 kJ/mol. [Iron pyrite: 4FeS + 6O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 4SO₂]
Stage 2 — Purification: As₂O₃ (catalyst poison) removed by Fe(OH)₃: As₂O₃ + 2Fe(OH)₃ → 2FeAsO₃ + 3H₂O. Dust and moisture also removed.
Stage 3 — Contact Tower: SO₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ SO₃, ΔH = −98.98 kJ/mol; V₂O₅ catalyst; 420–450 °C; 1–2 atm. V₂O₅ redox cycle: V⁵⁺ reduced to V⁴⁺ by SO₂; V⁴⁺ reoxidised to V⁵⁺ by O₂.
Stage 4 — Absorption: SO₃ + H₂SO₄(98.5%) → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum); then H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. Direct dissolution avoided (violent exotherm; mist formed).

parts.label: CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF H₂SO₄
points: Autoprotolysis: 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ H₃SO₄⁺ + HSO₄⁻, K = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴
Ionisation: 1st step (pKa1 = −2) complete — strong acid; 2nd step (pKa2 = 1.92) partial — HSO₄⁻ is weak acid
Dehydrating agent: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂SO₄ → 12C + 11H₂O (sucrose charring); C₂H₅OH →(H₂SO₄, 170°C) C₂H₄ + H₂O
Reaction with NaCl: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl(g)
Non-oxidising with active metals (dilute): Zn + dil.H₂SO₄ → H₂ + ZnSO₄
Oxidising agent (hot concentrated only): Cu + 2H₂SO₄(hot,conc.) → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O — S reduced from +6 to +4

quiz.q: The bond enthalpy of the N≡N triple bond is:
quiz.exp: N≡N triple bond enthalpy = +944 kJ/mol — one of the highest known, making N₂ kinetically inert.

quiz.q: The Kb of ammonia in water is:
quiz.exp: Kb(NH₃) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Very small → NH₃ is a weak base; equilibrium lies far to the left.

quiz.q: Which drying agent is used for ammonia gas in the laboratory?
quiz.exp: CaO (quicklime) is basic and does not react with NH₃. CaCl₂ forms a complex; H₂SO₄ and P₂O₅ are acidic and react with NH₃.

quiz.q: Which nitrogen oxide is known as laughing gas?
quiz.exp: N₂O (nitrous oxide) is called laughing gas. Used as dental anaesthetic and propellant. Oxidation state of N = +1.

quiz.q: The oxidation state of N in NO₂ is:
The noble metals used in a three-way catalytic converter are:
quiz.exp: Pt (platinum), Pd (palladium), and Rh (rhodium) are used. Pt/Rh for NOₓ reduction; Pt/Pd for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.

quiz.q: Which temperature range is correct for denitrification?
quiz.exp: Denitrification: 26–38 °C. Nitrification: 20–30 °C. Denitrification is the 'demanding' process — higher temperature than nitrification.

quiz.q: The allotrope S₈ of sulfur has which geometric shape?
quiz.exp: Cyclo-octasulfur (S₈) is a crown-shaped puckered ring of 8 S atoms, each connected to neighbours by single S-S bonds.

quiz.q: Sulfur can exhibit +4 and +6 oxidation states due to:
quiz.exp: Period 3 sulfur has vacant 3d orbitals. Electrons promoted from 3s/3p into 3d give excited states with 4 or 6 unpaired electrons → +4 and +6 states. Oxygen lacks accessible d orbitals.

quiz.q: The oxidation state of S in SO₃ is:
quiz.exp: In SO₃: x + 3(−2) = 0 → x = +6. Sulfur is in its maximum oxidation state.

quiz.q: Which reaction shows sulfur acting as an OXIDISING agent?
quiz.exp: In 2Cu + S → Cu₂S, copper is oxidised (0 → +1) by sulfur. Sulfur accepts electrons → oxidising agent. In (a), (c), (d), sulfur itself is oxidised.

quiz.q: Correct formula for gypsum is:
quiz.exp: Gypsum = CaSO₄·2H₂O (calcium sulfate dihydrate). CaSO₄·½H₂O = plaster of Paris; CaSO₄ = anhydrite. The book erroneously states CaSO₄·5H₂O.

quiz.q: The percentage of sulfur in gunpowder by mass is:
quiz.exp: Gunpowder: 75% KNO₃ + 15% C + 10% S. Sulfur is 10% — acts as additional fuel and accelerates burning.

quiz.q: The catalyst and working temperature in the Contact Process are:
quiz.exp: V₂O₅ at 420–450 °C and 1–2 atm. This is a compromise temperature — acceptable rate with reasonable yield.

quiz.q: Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) has the formula:
quiz.exp: Oleum = H₂S₂O₇ (pyrosulfuric acid): H₂SO₄ + SO₃ → H₂S₂O₇.

quiz.q: The self-ionisation of H₂SO₄ gives:
quiz.exp: Autoprotolysis: 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ H₃SO₄⁺ + HSO₄⁻, K = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴. One H₂SO₄ donates H⁺ to another.

quiz.q: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidises Cu to produce:
quiz.exp: Cu + 2H₂SO₄(hot, conc.) → CuSO₄ + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O. Cu oxidised (0 → +2); S reduced (+6 → +4). Cu does not react with dilute H₂SO₄.

quiz.q: The concentration of H₂SO₄ in lead-acid storage batteries is:
quiz.exp: Lead-acid batteries use 35.67% H₂SO₄ solution. Concentrated 98% H₂SO₄ would be too corrosive and reactive.

quiz.q: PAN is formed in the final step when peroxyacyl radical reacts with:
quiz.exp: Final step: RC(=O)OO• + NO₂ → RC(O)OONO₂ (PAN). Peroxyacyl radical combines with NO₂.

quiz.q: The pKa1 of H₂SO₄ is −2. This means the first ionisation is:
opts: Partial — equilibrium lies to the left
Complete — H₂SO₄ is a strong acid in its first dissociation
quiz.exp: Negative pKa means Ka >> 1. The first ionisation H₂SO₄ → H₃O⁺ + HSO₄⁻ is essentially complete (strong acid step). The second ionisation (HSO₄⁻, pKa2 = 1.92) is partial — HSO₄⁻ is a weak acid.
